blocks.text: A reply to the objections that can be made to the preceding chapter.

Since we have so far proved that רחם racham is the vulture, some objections seem possible from which it would follow that it is a bird different from the vulture. First, the Arabs, when they define the racham, say expressly that it is an eagle. Alkazuinius: رخمة طاير النسر [rakhma ṭāyir al-nasr] "The rachama is the eagle bird", that is, of the eagle kind. Alcamus: الانوق العقاب الرخمة [al-anūq al-ʿuqāb al-rakhma] "Anuk, eagle, rachama." Accordingly, in Alkazuinius [col. 312] the rachama, when about to give birth, is said to bring from India a stone that has another stone in its belly and relieves the pains of birth, that is, the ἀετίτης [aetitēs] stone, or eagle-stone. For it is described thus. Pliny, book 10, chapter 3: "This stone is pregnant, another stone sounding within, in its womb, when you shake it." Dioscorides, book 5: Ἀετίτης λίθος, ὁ ἐν τῷ κινεῖσθαι ἦχον ἀποτελῶν, ὡς ἑτέρου ἐγκύμων λίθου ὑπάρχων· [Aetitēs lithos, ho en tō kineisthai ēchon apotelōn, hōs heterou enkymōn lithou hyparchōn] "The eagle-stone, which makes a sound when moved, as though pregnant with another stone conceived within it." And a little later: Ἐν δὲ τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἀποτέξεως, περίαπτε τῷ μηρῷ, καὶ ἐκτὸς ὠδίνων τέξεται. [En de tō kairō tēs apotexeōs, periapte tō mērō, kai ektos ōdinōn texetai] "At the hour of birth tie it to the thigh (of the woman in labour), and she will give birth without pain." Chrysermus in Stobaeus, Discourse 98: Ἐν Εὐφράτῃ, ποταμῷ τῆς Παρθίας, γεννᾶται λίθος ἀετίτης καλούμενος· ὃν αἱ μαῖαι ταῖς δυστοκούσαις ἐπὶ τὰς γαστέρας ἐπιτιθέασι, καὶ παραχρῆμα τίκτουσιν ἄτερ ἀλγηδόνος. [En Euphratē, potamō tēs Parthias, gennatai lithos aetitēs kaloumenos; hon hai maiai tais dystokousais epi tas gasteras epititheasi, kai parachrēma tiktousin ater algēdonos] "In the Euphrates, a river of Parthia, a stone is produced called aëtides, which midwives place on the bellies of women in difficult labour, and at once they give birth without pain." Further, since the Greeks call it ἀετίτης [aetitēs], or eagle-stone, from the eagle, and not γυπίτης [gypitēs], or vulture-stone, from the vulture, it seems to follow that this stone is brought by the eagle, not by the vulture. And this is what the ancient writers assert. Pliny, in the place cited: "In the nests of the first three kinds of eagles and of the fifth the aëtites stone is built in." And book 30, ch. 14: "The aëtites stone, found in the nest of the eagle." And book 36, chapter 21: "The aëtites stone has great fame from the meaning of its name. [III, 66] It is found in the nests of eagles." Sextus: "The eagle's stone is found in its belly or nest." Isidore, Origines, book 16, chapter 5: "Aëtites (read Aëtitae) stones are found in the nests of eagles." Horus on the eagle, book 2, chapter 46: Ἐκεῖνος ἀπὸ θαλάττης, ἢ ἀπὸ γῆς λίθον ἐπαίρει, καὶ τίθησιν εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν νεοττίαν· [Ekeinos apo thalattēs, ē apo gēs lithon epairei, kai tithēsin eis tēn idian neottian] "It takes up a stone from the land or the sea and brings it into its own nest." Philostratus, book 2, chapter 7: Τὰ δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων τίς οὐκ οἶδεν, ὡς ἀετοὶ μὲν, καὶ πελαργοὶ, καλιὰς οὐκ ἂν πήξαιντο, μὴ πρότερον αὐταῖς ἐναρμόσαντες, ὁ μὲν τὸν ἀετίτην λίθον, ὁ δὲ τὸν λυχνίτην; [Ta de tōn ornithōn tis ouk oiden, hōs aetoi men, kai pelargoi, kalias ouk an pēxainto, mē proteron autais enarmosantes, ho men ton aetitēn lithon, ho de ton lychnitēn] "Who does not know what birds do: that eagles and storks never build their nests without placing stones in them, the former the aëtites, the latter the lychnites stone?" Aelian too, History, book 1, chapter 35, writes that eagles place in their nests τὸν λίθον, ὅσπερ οὖν ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀετίτης κέκληται [ton lithon, hosper oun ex autōn aetitēs keklētai], "the stone which is called aquiline after them." But the Arabs themselves also teach that this stone is found in the eagle's nest. Damir, in the chapter on العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] Alokab, which is a species of eagle: حجر العقاب حجر يشبه نوي التمر هندي اذا حرك سمع له صوي فاذا كسر لا يري فيه شي يوجد في عش العقاب والعقاب يجلبه من بلد الهند [ḥajar al-ʿuqāb ḥajar yushbih nawā al-tamr hindī idhā ḥurrika sumiʿa lahu ṣawī fa-idhā kusira lā yurā fīhi shay yūjad fī ʿushsh al-ʿuqāb wa-l-ʿuqāb yajlibuhu min balad al-hind] "The stone of alokab (or of the eagle) is a stone like the kernel of the tamarind; when it is moved a sound is heard, yet when it is broken nothing is seen in it. It is found in the nest of alokab (the eagle). And alokab (the eagle) brings it from India." And Alkazuinius himself, in the chapter On نسر [nasr], or the eagle: اذا كان اوان بيضها فالنسر الذكر يمشي الي بلاد الهند وياتي بحجر يوجد في [col. 313] بعض جبالها ويترك تحت الانثي لتخف عليه الالم [idhā kāna awān bayḍihā fa-l-nasr al-dhakar yamshī ilā bilād al-hind wa-yaʾtī bi-ḥajar yūjad fī baʿḍ jibālihā wa-yutrak taḥt al-unthā li-takhiff ʿalayhi al-alam] "When the eagle is about to lay its eggs, the male goes off to India and brings from there a stone that is found in some mountains of that land, and places it under the female to relieve her pains." Therefore, since in the same Alkazuinius the bird rachama is said to bring this very stone from India, he seems altogether to have taken the rachama for a true eagle. Third, since we have proved, both from reasons and from the authority of the ancients, that in the list of forbidden birds דיה daja is the vulture, if רחם racham is also the vulture, the same bird will be forbidden twice by Moses under different names in the same sequence of discourse, which does not seem tolerable. Fourth, it can be said that there is nothing in the vulture that answers to the name רחם, derived from mercy and natural στοργή [storgē] towards the young, since the vulture is a rapacious and carnivorous bird,
